newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia tackles NATO, Mideast role in busy week.
newsitem.headline: Russia tackles NATO, Mideast role in busy week.

text.p: Russia starts a week of talks with foreign leaders on Tuesday which it hopes will help break the impasse over NATO's plans to expand eastwards and promote Moscow's role on the world stage.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, Italian counterpart Lamberto Dini and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will bring one essential message in separate visits -- that NATO enlargement into eastern Europe does not threaten Russia.

Moscow will also hope to use a two-day visit by Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, starting on Tuesday, to raise its profile in the Middle East. It is a joint sponsor of the peace process with the United States but is overshadowed by Washington.

Moscow's hopes of success look slim. Russia has no clear way to increase its influence in the Middle East and both sides are sceptical of the chances of progress in the NATO enlargement row, although they welcome the start of real dialogue.

"The 'dialogue of the deaf' is ending. The time of practical dialogue, contact diplomacy, is starting," Vladimir Lukin, head of the Russian lower house of parliament's foreign affairs comittee, wrote of the dispute with NATO.
But, summing up the foreign policy problems facing Moscow five years after the collapse of the Soviet Union, he wrote in a newspaper article: "This is a very difficult time."
The meetings give Yeltsin, 66, the opportunity to continue his return to the world stage after pneumonia and heart surgery. He is due to meet Arafat on Tuesday and Albright on Friday.
Foreign policy has appeared to go on hold in the last seven months, most of which Yeltsin has spent out of the Kremlin.
Khairi Nadji Abdul-Fattah Aloridi, the Palestinian ambassador to Russia, told Interfax news agency that Moscow had "unused reserves for stepping up its role in the middle East peace process".

But Moscow has less influence in the region than in Soviet days, and had little to do with the recent U.S.-brokered peace deal under which Israel agreed to hand over 80 percent of the town of Hebron to the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
"The recent changes in the region, including the signing of the Hebron agreement, to a large extent happened without Russia's participation," the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper commented.
"After giving no help in settling this aspect of the problem (Hebron), Russian diplomacy is trying to show itself in the next stage of the peace process."
The visits by Kinkel on Tuesday and Wednesday, Dini on Thursday and Albright on Thursday and Friday coincide with a fierce Russian verbal offensive against NATO enlargement.

A Western diplomat in Moscow held out little hope of a breakthrough at the talks, which are a prelude for meetings between Primakov and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on February 23 and a Russian-U.S. summit next month.
"I would not say that the foreign ministers will have anything extraordinary in their baggage when they come to Moscow this week," said the diplomat, whose country is a NATO member.
Moscow says NATO membership for former members of the Warsaw Pact will threaten Russia's security, provide ammunition for Yeltsin's political foes and create divisions in Europe.

Russian officials are seeking as many concessions as possible, preferably before a NATO summit in July at which the alliance is expected to issue formal membership invitations to Poland, Hungary and the Czech repoublic.
Russia's wants a binding agreement giving Russia a say in issues affecting its security. NATO has balked at the demand.

Outlining ideas which might soften the blow of expansion, Primakov said in a television interview on Sunday that he would welcome a ban on movements of conventional troops across borders and ceilings on each country's weaponry.
